description: Religious experience, the design argument, and Aquinas's First Three Ways as Catholic evidence for God.
content_html:
Religious Experience as Evidence for God

Religious experience refers to moments when a person feels they have encountered God directly. Catholics believe such experiences are a genuine route to knowledge of God, though the Church exercises caution — not every claimed experience is accepted as authentic. The Catechism of the Catholic Church at paragraphs 66–67 teaches that although God’s revelation in Christ is complete, private revelations and religious experiences can “help us live more fully by it” in a particular era. Crucially, the Catechism makes clear that no new public revelation is possible after Jesus: private religious experiences cannot add to or override the deposit of faith.

Atheists and Humanists challenge the evidential value of religious experiences. They argue that a subjective inner experience — however powerful — is not verifiable evidence that God exists. The same brain states that produce a religious experience could, in their view, be produced by meditation, sleep deprivation, or psychological suggestion. Dawkins argues in The God Delusion that religious experience reflects the brain’s tendency to detect agency and pattern, not a real encounter with God. Catholics respond that the moral transformation, lasting peace, and convergence across cultures of religious experiences point to something real beyond neurological processes.

Key Fact

Catechism of the Catholic Church 66–67 teaches that God’s revelation is complete in Christ, but private revelations (including religious experiences) can help believers live more fully by it. The Church insists that no private revelation adds to the deposit of faith — it can only deepen understanding of what has already been revealed.

The Design Argument

The design argument (also called the teleological argument) proposes that the order, complexity and beauty of the natural world are best explained by an intelligent designer. Paul states in Romans 1:18–24 that “since the creation of the world God’s invisible qualities — his eternal power and divine nature — have been clearly seen, being understood from what has been made.” For Catholics, this verse establishes that the natural world itself reveals God to those who look carefully.

The most celebrated version of the design argument comes from William Paley, who published Natural Theology in 1802. Paley argued using the watchmaker analogy: if you found a watch on a heath, you would conclude it had a designer because of its intricate, purposeful construction. Paley argued that living organisms — eyes, hearts, wings — are far more complex than any watch. They must therefore have a designer vastly more intelligent than any human craftsman: God.

Richard Dawkins, in The Blind Watchmaker (1986), argues that natural selection entirely explains apparent design without any designer. Evolution shows that complexity can accumulate gradually through random mutation and differential survival — no intelligence is required. Dawkins calls Paley “gloriously and utterly wrong.” Humanists add that the natural world also contains enormous amounts of what looks like bad design: vestigial organs, disease, predation, extinction. If a designer made the universe, they argue, it is not an all-loving, all-powerful God. Catholics respond that evolution is compatible with Catholic teaching (the Church does not reject it) and that the laws of physics governing evolution still point to a lawgiver. Cardinal Newman famously argued that the orderliness of the cosmos — the fact that evolution follows predictable laws — is itself evidence of a rational mind behind nature.

Aquinas’s First Three Ways: The Cosmological Argument

The cosmological argument argues that the existence of the universe requires a cause outside itself. The most celebrated Catholic version comes from Thomas Aquinas, whose Summa Theologica presents five arguments. The spec focuses on the first three, which are all forms of the cosmological argument.

Key Fact

Aquinas’s First Three Ways are: (1) the argument from motion (everything in motion was put in motion by something else — there must be an unmoved mover, God); (2) the argument from causation (everything has a cause — there must be a first uncaused cause, God); (3) the argument from contingency (things in the universe exist but might not — there must be a necessary being, God, who cannot fail to exist). All three are a posteriori: they begin from observation of the world and reason to God.

The prime mover is the conclusion of the First Way. Aquinas observed that everything in the universe is in motion or in a state of change. For something to change, it must be acted upon by something already in the relevant state. You cannot have an infinite chain going backwards — at some point, there must be something that initiates motion without itself being moved. This first mover is what Catholics call God. The argument from contingency takes a different angle: the universe did not have to exist. Its existence demands explanation; that explanation is a being whose existence is necessary rather than contingent — God.

Students regularly confuse three distinct philosophical arguments. Aquinas’s First Three Ways are a posteriori (starting from observation of the world: motion, causation, contingency) and conclude to God as first mover, first cause, and necessary being. The Ontological Argument, by contrast, was devised by St Anselm of Canterbury in his Proslogion (c.1078) and is a priori (based on the concept of God alone, not observation). Anselm’s argument is NOT in the Edexcel spec for Paper 3 — do not bring it in. The Kalam cosmological argument (“everything that begins to exist has a cause; the universe began to exist; therefore the universe has a cause”) is the Islamic version associated with al-Ghazali — covered in the Islam route, not here. Aquinas and al-Ghazali made different arguments and lived in different centuries. Never attribute the Kalam to Aquinas or the Five Ways to al-Ghazali.
exam_tip_html: The most common error on questions about the cosmological argument is confusing Aquinas’s First Three Ways with the Ontological Argument (Anselm) or the Kalam (al-Ghazali). For this paper, you need Aquinas: First Way (motion), Second Way (causation), Third Way (contingency). These are all observations from the world, not logical proofs from the concept of God alone. For the 5-mark source question, Romans 1:18–24 is the named anchor for the design argument: cite the book, chapter and verse range. For the 12-mark Discuss, develop the Dawkins/evolution challenge in full — do not just mention it in passing — and respond to it from the Catholic position. SPaG marks reward precise spelling of: cosmological, contingency, teleological.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Catholics believe religious experiences are genuine encounters with God, guided by Catechism 66–67 — but private revelations cannot add to Christian doctrine, only deepen it.
  • The design argument (Paley’s watchmaker analogy, Romans 1:18–24) argues that the complexity and order of nature point to an intelligent creator; Dawkins counters that evolution explains complexity without a designer.
  • Aquinas’s First Three Ways (motion, causation, contingency) are a posteriori arguments concluding to God as prime mover, first cause and necessary being — distinct from Anselm’s Ontological Argument and al-Ghazali’s Kalam.

practice_questions.text: Outline three features of Aquinas's cosmological argument for the existence of God.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each of three discrete points from: everything in motion was put in motion by something else, so there must be an unmoved mover (1); everything has a cause, so there must be a first uncaused cause (1); contingent things could have not existed, so there must be a necessary being (1). Three distinct points required.

Up to 3 marks: Paley argued that if you found a watch on a heath, its complexity would imply a watchmaker (1); he applied this to living organisms such as the eye, which are even more complex and purposeful than a watch (1); therefore the natural world must also have a designer — God (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Catholics use religious experience as evidence for the existence of God.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason (1 for a stated point, 2 for a developed explanation). For example: Religious experiences produce lasting moral transformation and peace, suggesting they originate from God rather than the human mind alone (2); The Catechism (CCC 66-67) recognises that private revelations, though adding nothing to doctrine, can deepen faith and help believers live more fully by God's revelation (2). Other valid reasoning accepted.

practice_questions.text: Explain two Catholic reasons for believing the design argument supports belief in God, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason with development; 1 mark for a named source. Example: The natural world shows clear evidence of order and purpose — eyes, ecosystems, physical constants — which is best explained by an intelligent creator rather than chance (2); Romans 1:18-24 explicitly states that God's eternal power and divine nature have been 'clearly seen' in the created world, lending scriptural support to the design argument (2); source credit for naming Romans 1:18-24 (1).

practice_questions.text:
'The cosmological argument is the most convincing proof of the existence of God.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; explicit weighing of arguments; justified conclusion. May argue the cosmological argument is strong because it begins from observable facts (not mere logic) and Aquinas's Three Ways are logically coherent, but evaluate whether it is more or less convincing than the design argument or religious experience; address Humanist and atheist rebuttals (infinite regress question, 'who made God' objection). Secure (7-9): Both sides present, at least one source, conclusion present but evaluative language limited. Developing (4-6): One side dominant, vague sources, descriptive conclusion. Emerging (1-3): Brief, one-sided, no sources. SPaG: cosmological, contingency, Aquinas, teleological.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why some people argue the design argument does not prove God exists, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Darwin's theory of evolution (On the Origin of Species, 1859) shows that complexity in living organisms arises through natural selection, not design — Dawkins argues this removes the need for a designer (2); the presence of suffering, disease and extinction in nature looks like poor design, making it hard to attribute the world to an all-loving, all-powerful God (2); source credit for naming Romans 1:18-24 in counter-argument framing, or naming Dawkins The Blind Watchmaker, or Darwin (1).

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following correctly describes Aquinas's Second Way?
options: Everything in motion needs something to move it — so there is an unmoved mover
Everything has a cause — so there must be a first uncaused cause
Contingent things might not exist — so a necessary being must exist
The complexity of nature implies an intelligent designer

knowledge_checks.q: What does the Catechism of the Catholic Church (paragraphs 66-67) teach about private revelations?
options: They add new doctrine to the Christian faith
They are never trustworthy and must always be rejected
They can help believers live more fully by God's completed revelation in Christ
They are only valid if approved by the Pope personally

knowledge_checks.q: William Paley argued in his _____ analogy that the complexity of nature implies a divine designer.
Romans 1:18-24 teaches that God's 'invisible qualities' have been 'clearly seen' in what has been _____ since the creation of the world.
Match each of Aquinas's First Three Ways to its starting observation:
right: Everything in motion is moved by something else
Things exist but might not — they are contingent

flashcard_questions.q: What is Aquinas's First Way, and what does it conclude?
flashcard_questions.a: The argument from motion: everything moved needs a mover; there must be an unmoved mover — God.

flashcard_questions.q: What is Aquinas's Third Way, and what does it conclude?
flashcard_questions.a: The argument from contingency: things might not exist; there must be a necessary being — God.

flashcard_questions.q: Who wrote Natural Theology (1802) and what analogy did it introduce?
flashcard_questions.a: William Paley; the watchmaker analogy — complexity in nature implies a designer, as a watch implies a watchmaker.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Romans 1:18-24 say about the natural world and God?
flashcard_questions.a: That God's eternal power and divine nature have been 'clearly seen' in what has been made since creation.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Catechism of the Catholic Church's teaching on religious experience (CCC 66-67)?
flashcard_questions.a: Private revelations can help believers live more fully by God's revelation in Christ, but add nothing new to doctrine.

flashcard_questions.q: What is Richard Dawkins's main objection to the design argument?
flashcard_questions.a: Natural selection explains biological complexity without a designer — evolution is a 'blind watchmaker'.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'a posteriori' mean, and why does it apply to Aquinas's Three Ways?
flashcard_questions.a: Based on observation of the world — the Three Ways begin from motion, causation and contingency in nature.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the 'prime mover' in Aquinas's First Way?
flashcard_questions.a: The being that initiates all motion without itself being moved — identified by Aquinas with God.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the 'contingency' argument in Aquinas's Third Way?
flashcard_questions.a: Contingent things could have not existed; a necessary being (God) must exist to explain why anything exists at all.

flashcard_questions.q: How do Catholics respond to the 'who made God' objection to the cosmological argument?
flashcard_questions.a: God is a necessary being — unlike contingent things, God does not require a cause; he cannot fail to exist.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the design argument also called, and why?
flashcard_questions.a: The teleological argument — from the Greek telos (purpose), because it focuses on apparent purpose in nature.

flashcard_questions.q: Which argument is associated with Anselm of Canterbury, and why is it NOT on this course?
flashcard_questions.a: The Ontological Argument (a priori, from the concept of God alone) — not in the spec; Aquinas's Ways are the focus.

glossary_terms.definition: A direct personal encounter with what the person believes to be God or the divine, which may include awe, vision, or a sense of union with a greater power.
A philosophical argument for God's existence based on the apparent order, complexity and purpose found in the natural world.
An eighteenth-century English theologian who argued in Natural Theology (1802) that the complexity of nature, like a watch, implies a divine designer.
Paley's argument that just as a watch implies a watchmaker because of its complexity, so nature's complexity implies God.
A philosophical argument for God's existence based on the existence of the universe, arguing it requires a first cause or prime mover.
A thirteenth-century Dominican friar and theologian whose Five Ways in the Summa Theologica provide five a posteriori arguments for God's existence.
In Aquinas's First Way, the being that initiates all motion without itself being moved — identified with God.
In Aquinas's Third Way, the observation that things exist but might not have — requiring a necessary being, God, to explain existence itself.
